passage: I'm Zubin, and I sit across from Ritu on the finance team. Last month our director changed the bonus pool so that the newest hire got nothing, even though the hire had done most of the closing work. Everyone saw it. Ritu did not say a word in the meeting. But afterwards she stayed late, and I noticed her drafting an email, deleting it, and drafting it again. She asked me quietly whether others felt the same, and over chai we spoke to two colleagues. Three days later she sent the director a short, careful note listing the facts and asking how the split was decided. I can't tell you whether she was scared or just being thorough. She did say once, "Saying nothing has a cost too." We all need this job.

qa.q: What did Ritu send to the director three days later?
qa.a: A short, careful note listing the facts and asking how the split was decided.

qa.q: What might Ritu have been worried about while drafting and deleting the email?
qa.a: Possibly the risk to her job, since speaking up could cost her, though Zubin admits it is hard to tell whether she was scared or just thorough.

qa.q: What could Ritu do if the director does not reply?
qa.a: Ask calmly for a short meeting, keep her written record, and lean on the two colleagues who share the concern.

qa.q: How might the newest hire see the bonus change?
qa.a: The newest hire may feel the closing work went unrecognised and may hope someone speaks up.

grounding: An observer sees a colleague who knows a decision is unfair weigh the risk, find allies and raise it calmly in writing.

"Did you see the new roster?" Charu asked, closing the pantry door.

"I saw." Trisha kept her voice low. "Every night shift for the next month goes to the three of us who joined this year. Mr. Bedi's favourites get none."

"That's unfair."

"I know it is." Trisha twisted her ID card. "But my brother's fees depend on this salary. If I complain and he decides I'm difficult..."

"So you'll just do thirty nights?"

Trisha was quiet. "Staying silent is a choice too, isn't it? And it has a cost. My health, for one."

"Then let's not do it alone. Arvind and Seema are on the same roster. Four of us, one calm email. Just facts, asking for a rotation."

"In writing?"

"In writing. Polite. Copy HR."

Trisha breathed out. "Okay. I'll draft it. You check the tone."

That night they sent it, four names at the bottom.

qa.q: Who gets every night shift for the next month?
qa.a: The three who joined this year get every night shift.

qa.q: Why was Trisha afraid to speak up?
qa.a: Trisha was afraid of being seen as difficult and losing the job, since her brother's fees depended on her salary.

qa.q: How did Trisha and Charu raise the concern safely?
qa.a: They weighed the risk, found allies on the same roster, and sent a calm, factual email in writing with HR copied.

qa.q: How does Charu see Trisha's fear of speaking up?
qa.a: Charu understands the fear but pushes gently, reminding her silence also has a cost and offering to share the risk.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young woman afraid to challenge an unfair decision because she needs the job, who weighs the risk, finds allies and raises the concern calmly in writing.

passage:
I'm Rafiq, and last year I learned that silence costs something too.

At the bank's back office, our manager decided that Kalyani, who had just come back from maternity leave, would be moved off the loans team to data entry. Same salary, no explanation. Everyone knew why. She'd "be distracted".

I knew it was unfair. I also knew I needed this job. My father's medicines, my sister's wedding next year. My stomach churned every time I thought of saying something.

So I thought it through. What could I lose? What would it cost to say nothing? I realised if I stayed quiet, I'd be telling myself I was that kind of man.

I spoke to two colleagues, Joseph and Anu, who felt the same. We wrote one calm email to HR, factual, not angry. "We are concerned the decision about Kalyani may not have been based on her work."

HR reviewed it. Kalyani was back on loans within a month.

qa.q: Where was Kalyani moved after maternity leave?
qa.a: She was moved off the loans team to data entry.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel when thinking about speaking up?
qa.a: Rafiq felt afraid, his stomach churning, because he needed the job for his family.

qa.q: How did Rafiq raise the concern while managing the risk?
qa.a: He weighed the risk honestly, found two allies, and sent one calm, factual email to HR.

qa.q: How might Kalyani have felt about being moved without explanation?
qa.a: Kalyani probably felt hurt and sidelined, judged for becoming a mother rather than for her work.

grounding: A first-person account shows a young man afraid to speak about an unfair decision because he needs the job, who weighs the risk, finds allies and raises it calmly in writing.
